newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - High German insolvencies ups reform pressure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - High German insolvencies ups reform pressure.

text.p: New data on Thursday showing that ever more German firms are going bust and fewer are being founded piled pressure on the Bonn government to achieve results in its bid to pass vital structural reforms.

Germany's Federal Statistics Office said that 2,004 firms opened insolvency proceedings in January, a rise of 7.3 percent on the same month a year earlier. The rise in insolvencies extended a four-year run of record company failures.
Research published by a business think-tank also showed that the number of new companies founded last year fell for the first time in a decade, by five percent to 502,000.

Meanwhile, 431,000 companies were liquidated, leaving a net increase in Germany's corporate population of 71,000 -- a rise which was over a third slower than in the previous year, the Institut fuer Mittelstandsforschung said.

Germany's problems are "too much state, too little market, excessive costs, over-regulation and too much bureaucracy," Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said in a parliament debate called by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
Rexrodt added it was vital to pass government tax and welfare reforms to create the conditions for a business revival and improve job prospects for Germany's 4.5 million unemployed.
Wage bargaining must also be decentralised and made more flexible, Rexrodt added. He rejected a call by the IG Metall industrial trade union to introduce a 32-hour working week.
"It is based on a false assumption, that we have a certain amount of work in our country that just needs to be shared out better," Rexrodt said.
Economists said the weak economy last year, when gross domestic product rose by just 1.4 percent, was only partly to blame for Germany's deepening corporate crisis.

Axel Nitschke, economist at the German Chamber of Industry and Trade (DIHT), said that excessive wage rises in the past in both formerly communist eastern Germany and in the richer west were forcing more and more companies out of business.
"Companies are slowly losing the air they need to breathe," Nitschke told Reuters.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government has launched ambitious reforms which would slash corporate taxes and clear away many of the tax breaks which hamper rational investment decisions.

But, lacking a majority in both houses of parliament, the government has been forced to negotiate with the SPD to seek a compromise. No breakthroughs have been achieved yet, although more talks have been set for April 23.
The political debate -- and risk that business tax reforms could be severely watered down -- is damaging both investment and business confidence.

Analysts said a fall in confidence shown by the Ifo institute's latest business survey was due in part to the tax wrangling. The Ifo index for western Germany fell to 92.4 in March from 93.6 in February.
"It is important to simplify and cut taxes as soon as possible. No subsidy programme can replace that," said Reinhard Clemens of the Institute fuer Mittelstandsforschung.

The DIHT fears that the SPD's call to reduce so-called labour overheads -- contributions for unemployment, health and pension schemes -- in a bid to create more jobs will simply end up being taken back in the form of hikes in indirect taxes.
"Our concern is that if taxes rise elsewhere then all the positive effects will be lost," Nitschke said.
